title: Dilucidationes super methodo elegantissima, qua illustris de la Grange usus est in integranda aequatione differentiali dx/√X = dy/√Y

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E506 is Euler's commentary on Lagrange's 1766–69 method for integrating dx/√X ± dy/√Y = 0. In Lagrange's method one introduces a parameter t, uses p = x+y and q = x−y, and integrates a second-order system. In the preceding sections Euler obtained two algebraic integrals for X = A + Cx² + Ex⁴. On the previous page the first is written with 2A + 2Cxy + 2Ex²y² on the left. The second, from §70, is [A(x²+y²) + 2Cx²y² + Ex²y²(x²+y²) ∓ 2xy√XY]/(x²−y²)² = A/k². Here k is the value of x when y = 0, and K is a constant defined earlier (not visible here).

(1) End of Corollary II. Substituting the expression for √XY from the second integral into the first gives a rational relation. Removing the factor (x−y)² gives (2A ∓ 2√AK)/k² = A(x+y)²/(k²xy) − Exy − A/(xy). Multiplying by k²xy and simplifying gives (A/k²)(x²+y²−k²) − Ex²y² ± (2xy√AK)/k² = 0. Euler notes this is exactly his old 'canonical' symmetric biquadratic, the algebraic form of the addition theorem: 0 = α + γ(x²+y²) + 2δxy + ζx²y², with α = −A/k², γ = A/k², 2δ = ±2√AK/k², ζ = −E. So Lagrange's route reproduces Euler's own addition-theorem relation. Both steps check out algebraically.

(2) Corollary III (§72). The 'second method' extends to a general quartic radicand with zero constant term:
dx/√(x(B+Cx+Dx²+Ex³)) ± dy/√(y(B+Cy+Dy²+Ey³)) = 0.
Its integral is [B(x+y) + 2Cxy + Dxy(x+y) + 2Ex²y² ∓ 2√(xy·P(x)P(y))]/(x−y)² = B/k, where P(x) = B+Cx+Dx²+Ex³. This is the familiar Euler–Lagrange integral ((√X ∓ √Y)/(x−y))² − E(x+y)² − D(x+y) = const, specialised to A = 0, with the constant C(x−y)²/(x−y)² absorbed. Expanding confirms the stated numerator. Putting y = 0, x = k gives the constant B/k.

(3) Replacing x, y by x², y² turns the equation into dx/√(B+Cx²+Dx⁴+Ex⁶) ± dy/√(B+Cy²+Dy⁴+Ey⁶) = 0. Its algebraic integral is [B(x²+y²) + 2Cx²y² + Dx²y²(x²+y²) + 2Ex⁴y⁴ ∓ 2xy√(X Y)]/(x²−y²)² = B/k². Euler presents this as an equation where the radicals 'rise to the sixth dimension'. The following pages re-derive it by Lagrange's p,q method, with X now an even sextic.
errors: Printing error in the original: inside the radical of the first integral of §72 the second factor is printed '(B + Cy + Dyy + Ay³)'; it should be '+ Ey³'.

Not an error, but a caveat: the 'much more general' sextic case is only apparently of higher genus. The radicand is an even sextic, and u = x² reduces dx/√(B+Cx²+Dx⁴+Ex⁶) to du/(2√(u(B+Cu+Du²+Eu³))), an elliptic differential. Euler in effect makes this substitution himself, in reverse. The page offers nothing genuinely hyperelliptic.

ideas.what: Eliminating the radical between two algebraic integrals of the same elliptic differential equation yields Euler's symmetric biquadratic α+γ(x²+y²)+2δxy+ζx²y²=0
ideas.modern_name: Euler's addition theorem for elliptic integrals (symmetric biquadratic / Euler's canonical relation)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (1750s–1760s, E251/E252 and later; Institutiones calculi integralis I)
ideas.where_published: Euler's papers on the addition theorem, e.g. E251, E252, and Institutiones calculi integralis vol. I

ideas.what: Algebraic integral ((√X∓√Y)/(x−y))² − E(x+y)² − D(x+y) = const for a general quartic X, here with zero constant term
ideas.modern_name: Lagrange's form of the algebraic integral of Euler's equation (addition formula for the Weierstrass/Jacobi functions)
ideas.where_published: Lagrange, Miscellanea Taurinensia IV; Euler E345, E506

ideas.what: Substitution x→x² converting a quartic-without-constant-term case into an even-sextic radicand
ideas.modern_name: Reduction of even hyperelliptic (genus 2 symmetric) differentials to elliptic ones via u = x²
ideas.usually_credited_to: Implicit in Euler/Legendre; systematic reductions by Legendre and Jacobi

deep.surprise_reason: All computations are correct and the results are classical: Euler's addition-theorem biquadratic and the Lagrange algebraic integral. The sextic generalization is an elliptic case in disguise, obtained by the substitution x→x². Nothing here is absent from the literature.
transcription_corrections: The original indeed prints 'B + Cy + Dyy + Ay³' in the radical of the first §72 integral. The transcription is faithful, but this is a misprint for 'Ey³'.
The '[?]' after '= B/k' can be removed: the image clearly reads '= B/k.'
In the line 'quae porro reducta et per (x−y)² diuisa' the transcription is correct; the left side reads (2A ∓ 2√AK)/kk.
